query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Steel corrosion resistance in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is enhanced by the formation of a uniform, protective oxide film that arises from suppressed grain-boundary elemental segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless steel alloys containing passivating elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, and minor amounts of Cu) that naturally exhibit varying degrees of grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments (e.g., optimized annealing) and adjust alloy chemistry to minimize grain-boundary segregation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to corrosive environments representative of chemical-processing (e.g., dilute acidic solutions) and nuclear-power applications (e.g., elevated temperature and irradiative conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: A homogenized grain-boundary microstructure that facilitates the continuous formation of a coherent, slow-growing oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Minimizing localized segregation prevents the formation of copper-rich or other deleterious precipitates at grain boundaries, thereby promoting an even distribution of passivating elements. This uniformity enables the development of a protective oxide film that reduces localized anodic dissolution and impedes corrosive ion ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples treated to reduce grain-boundary segregation will exhibit lower corrosion current densities, improved corrosion potentials, and more uniform passive film morphology compared to conventionally processed steels.
generation.baseline: Stainless steels produced with standard processing methods that result in notable elemental segregation at grain boundaries leading to discontinuous oxide films.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to steels with adequate levels of passivating elements (e.g., Cr, Ni) under moderate corrosive and thermal conditions; under extreme conditions (e.g., very high irradiation doses or highly aggressive chemistries), additional mechanisms may become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between the extent of segregation reduction and the degree of corrosion resistance improvement is not fully defined, and the impact of radiation on passivation mechanisms remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of stainless steel samples: one using standard processing yielding typical grain-boundary segregation, and another using an optimized annealing process designed to suppress segregation. Expose both sets to a corrosive environment (e.g., 0.5 M H2SO4 at room temperature) and simulate nuclear power conditions (elevated temperature with radiation exposure).
measurements: Electrochemical polarization to measure corrosion current density and corrosion potential
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess oxide film continuity and grain-boundary composition
Surface roughness and film thickness analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples processed to suppress segregation do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower corrosion current, higher corrosion potential, and more uniform oxide film) compared to the standard samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Effect of local chemical order on the irradiation-induced defect evolution in CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy

Abstract: SignificanceHigh-entropy alloys have emerged as promising structural materials for nuclear applications. Among the structural features of high-entropy alloys that may influence their irradiation response, a variable that has not received careful study so far is the internal local chemical order. By combining ion irradiation experiments and atomistic simulation of CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy, here we demonstrate that increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination. This finding opens an avenue to tailor radiation resistance, especially effective as the local chemical order are well suited to affect the evolution of point defects. Corrosion Resistance of Al0.5CoCrFeNiCuxAgy (x = 0.25, 0.5; y = 0, 0.1) High-Entropy Alloys in 0.5M H2SO4 Solution

Abstract: AbstractThe electrochemical behavior of the as-cast Al0.5CoCrFeNiCuxAgy (x = 0.25, 0.5; y = 0, 0.1) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in a 0.5M H2SO4 solution was studied. Polarization measurements were carried out in a standard three-electrode electrochemical cell at room temperature using a platinum counter electrode and a saturated silver chloride reference electrode. For Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.5 and Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.5Ag0.1, copper segregation along the grain boundaries was observed, which highly dissolved in the sulfuric acid solution and resulted in low corrosion resistance of the samples. Introducing Ag into Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.25 HEA led to the precipitation of a copper–silver eutectic structure, in which the copper regions were selectively dissolved in the sulfuric acid solution. Al0.5CoCrFeNiCu0.25 exhibited the best corrosion resistance with the corrosion current density of Icorr = 3.52 ± 0.02 μA/cm2, significantly superior to that of the Al0.5CoCrFeNi sample without copper and silver (Icorr = 6.05 ± 0.05 μA/cm2).
